entries.title: Amid pitching injuries, Cubs need Matthew Boyd to make big impact as summer goes on: ‘That’s our ace’
entries.summary: <p>What constitutes an ace? And whatever your definition, do the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> have one?</p><p>That’s a trickier question to answer now than it was a few months ago, as injuries have torn through the team’s pitching staff, with an entire rotation and late-inning mix of relievers simultaneously on the IL, including might-have-been aces like righties <b>Cade Horton</b>, <b>Ben Brown</b> and <b>Edward Cabrera</b>.</p><p>The trade deadline looms, with names as enticing as two-time reigning AL Cy Young winner <b>Tarik Skubal</b> possibly on the block. But team president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/07/31/2025-trade-deadline-cubs-prez-jed-hoyer-balks-at-asking-price-for-frontline-starter-adds-four-players" >shied away from trading for pitching last deadline</a>, citing an exorbitant price.</p><p>If the Cubs are going to have an ace the rest of the way, it might have to be <b>Matthew Boyd</b>.</p><p>That’s not a bad thing after the left-hander was an All Star last season. Heck, inside the clubhouse, he’s already got that title.</p><p>“You don’t know what one guy’s going to do,” center fielder <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> said last week in New York after Boyd made his first start back from the IL, “but the state that we’re in with what we need, in terms of pitching, that’s our ace and we’re glad that he’s back, man.</p><p>“That’s good news for us.”</p><p>Given the Cubs’ injury situation, Boyd returning to action has been huge. Though he’s been limited to fewer than 80 pitches in each of his last two starts as he builds back to full capacity, he’s been effective, allowing three runs in 9⅔ innings.</p><p>Boyd was excellent last season, but a couple injured-list trips have prevented a follow-up to this point. Tuesday’s outing was just his seventh start of the year.</p><p>The second half, though, can be his time to shine in a time of need for his team.</p><p>“This is 180 innings we got last year from Matt, and that means it’s a guy that makes every start, that you can count on, that single-handedly won some games for us going deep into games,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Tuesday. “That stability is something we sorely need and are going to need for the second half.”</p><p>Boyd is capable of pitching well enough to be talked about with the top arms in the league, posting a 3.21 ERA in 31 starts last season.</p><p>With the Cubs attempting to figure out a tricky pitching puzzle, Boyd can be a stabilizing force once again.</p><p>“My job is just to take the ball and go pitch every fifth day. It’s nothing outside of that,” Boyd said Tuesday. “All those things you’re saying [about providing stability] are awesome, but those are symptoms of doing what I’m supposed to do: taking the ball, regardless of the situation, going out there and just giving everything I’ve got on every single pitch.”</p><h3><b>Thumb struck</b></h3><p>Third baseman <b>Alex Bregman</b> saw his work pay off Tuesday with a big three-run homer. But he drew some attention online for what he did after the blast.</p><p>As he was rounding third base, Bregman gave a thumbs down. After crossing home plate, he did it again, this time toward the stands behind home plate, where the press box and broadcast booths are located.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">WAY back, WAY gone. <a href="https://t.co/8cjIPjW7lk">pic.twitter.com/8cjIPjW7lk</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2072119833559183525?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 1, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><p>Bregman followed by posting a picture of his home run on Instagram, complete with a thumbs-down emoji.</p><p>Two days earlier, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/29/cubs-alex-bregman-bobbled-ball-hustle-jim-deshaies-slump-power-slugging-percentage-batting-average-free-agent-signing-jed-hoyer" >Bregman stirred up anger among fans</a> already frustrated by his lack of production by not running full speed on a bobbled ground ball, receiving an on-air admonishment of sorts from announcer <b>Jim Deshaies</b>.</p><p>Asked Wednesday what the thumbs-down celebration was, Bregman responded, “Nothing.”</p><p>Asked if it was a message to anybody, he said, “No.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel entries.title: Workers brave extreme temperatures as heat wave stretches on in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>While many have been able to remain indoors during the heat wave, countless Chicago workers have continued to endure sweltering conditions as extreme temperatures persist throughout the week.</p><p>Faheem Jackson, working construction in Douglas on Wednesday, is among many workers doing their best to make it through the day as temperatures climbed into the 90s and the heat index reached nearly 100 degrees.</p><p>“There is no staying cool right now,” said Jackson, 34. “The heat is no joke.”</p><p>Jackson, in his third construction season, hydrated and taken breaks in the shade to find some relief.</p><p>“I just try not to think about the time as it goes by,” he said.</p><p>Wednesday marked the fourth consecutive day of a heat wave that brought dangerously hot and humid conditions to much of the area. </p><p>An extreme heat warning remained in effect through early Friday, with temperatures expected to stay in the 90s throughout the week and heat indexes reaching up to 105 Tuesday and Wednesday, according to the National Weather Service. Temperatures soared to 95 Wednesday — still 8 degrees shy of the day's record set in 1956, but 11 degrees above average — with a low of 80 reached around 5:30 a.m. </p><div class="Enhancement" The Calmuet City resident has been working in construction for three seasons.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>And even more workers were out on the roads than usual. The Illinois Department of Transportation warned drivers to be aware of pavement failures on roads due to the brutal heat, and also to look out for crews trying to make quick emergency repairs.</p><p>"While it’s impossible to predict where or when these failures might occur, maintenance personnel will be monitoring road conditions and on standby to make repairs as quickly as possible when they are observed and reported," the agency said in a statement. "The public is advised to anticipate slowing traffic and move over for workers and other emergency personnel when repairs are being made."</p><p>For those who have to be in the heat, the <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/topics-services/environmental-health-protection/hot-weather.html" target="_blank" >Illinois Department of Health suggests</a> wearing loose, light-colored, cotton clothing, avoid direct sunlight when possible and taking regularly scheduled rest periods to hydrate. The health department also suggests using a buddy system when working outside, as heat-related illness can develop quickly and "with or without feelings of discomfort" first.</p><p>In suburban Riverside, trash pickup was scheduled to start early Thursday to avoid workers still being out when the heat index value peaks at noon.</p><p>Laurence Rivers Jr., who corrals shopping carts at a Mariano’s in Bronzeville, told the Sun-Times he’s been staying cool by going inside the store for breaks.</p><p>“I go in and I get some water and some freeze pops,” said Rivers, who was holding an orange-flavored freezer pop in his mouth while corralling the carts.</p><p>Thunderstorms were expected to move through the area Thursday night and continue into the July 4 holiday weekend, weather officials said. The storms would offer slight temperature drops into the 80s, though conditions would remain hot and humid.</p><p>It could be plenty uncomfortable indoors for some Chicagoans, too.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/chicago/latest/chicago_il/0-0-0-2676238#JD_14X-8-803" target="_blank" >2022 city ordinance</a> requires some buildings, including senior centers, nursing homes, and high rises more than 80 feet tall or buildings with more than 100 units, to provide air conditioning in common areas when the heat index is over 80 degrees. And in nursing homes and senior centers, air conditioning must be provided for all rooms.</p><p>Even so, some of those buildings have generated the most 3-1-1 complaints about no air conditioning during this week’s heat wave, according to a WBEZ analysis.</p><p>That includes three complaints each from two Chicago Housing Authority buildings: Lincoln Perry Apartments, 240 W. 107th Place, and Holland House, 3245 S. Prairie Ave.</p><p>As of Wednesday afternoon, the city had received nearly 60 complaints this week about no air conditioning.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/06/30/chicago-heat-wave-extreme-weather-brandon-johnson-health-south-side-west-side" >As temperatures soar, city urged to add nighttime cooling options for vulnerable residents</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/30/extreme-heat-warning-hot-weather-cooling-centers-forecast-power-outages" >Heat wave with temps in the 90s expected all week in Chicago; heat warning extended</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The heat was also impacting the energy grid, as widespread air conditioning use surged electricity demand. </p><p>ComEd activated its "voluntary load reduction" program Wednesday, which asks high-consumption commercial and industrial customers — as well as some residential customers — to reduce electricity use during peak usage hours.</p><p>The energy company suggests covering windows and having fans spin counter-clockwise to increase airflow and reduce the need for air conditioning, while also turning thermostats to a warmer temperature when away from home. Any devices not being used, including electric lights, should ideally be unplugged, officials said. </p><p>"We have crews ready to respond quickly and safely to any service interruptions, and we are working hard behind the scenes to keep the power flowing during what is shaping up to be a dangerous stretch of heat," said David Perez, executive vice-president and COO of entries.title: Can Illinois’ newest state agency improve early childhood services? Officials hope so.
entries.summary: <p>Parents in Illinois who have long navigated a fragmented system to find daycare, preschool and other early childhood services can now look under one roof for the assistance they need.</p><p>That’s due to the new Illinois Department of Early Childhood, which officially launched Wednesday with the aim <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/01/26/many-challenges-ahead-as-illinois-unifies-early-childhood-programs-report-finds" target="_blank" ><u>of untangling the work</u></a> that was previously done by three state agencies.</p><p>The new agency is responsible for a range of state programs, including those that offer home visiting and early intervention services for babies and toddlers with development delays. It will also license and provide quality ratings for early learning programs. Part of the shift involved transitioning over $1 billion in funds to a new unified grant system.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-hangRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-credit"><p>Illinois Department of Early Childhood</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Teresa Ramos, the secretary of the new agency, said families who are currently participating in these programs shouldn’t expect any changes to their services. But parents looking for care can now visit a <a class="Link" href="https://idec.illinois.gov/idec-education-care-transition-planning/faqs.html" target="_blank" ><u>new unified website</u></a>.</p><p>“There's one place to go, a place to ask questions, a place to get answers and to be connected directly to services,” Ramos said.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker called for the new agency in 2023 and signed a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/06/25/jb-pritzker-new-state-agency-early-education" target="_blank" ><u>law creating the department</u></a> in 2024. Illinois is the latest state to <a class="Link" href="https://www.the74million.org/zero2eight/why-are-state-departments-of-early-childhood-education-so-trendy-right-now/" target="_blank" ><u>establish a standalone department</u></a> for early care and education, joining a dozen other states that already have them.</p><p>State officials hope it will solve the challenges that families faced as they assessed their early learning options. With services spread across different agencies, some parents had to fill out duplicate forms. And it was difficult for families to get an overall picture of where quality programs existed because multiple entities were responsible for monitoring that.</p><p>Ramos will be in charge of 550 staffers and shepherd a<a class="Link" href="https://idec.illinois.gov/news/2026/approved-budget-creates-new-milestone-for-families-and-early-chi.html" target="_blank" ><u> $4.4 billion budget</u></a> approved by the state legislature for early childhood education and care. That includes 340 staff transferring from the state’s Department of Children and Family Services, the Department of Human Services and the State Board of Education.</p><p>Ramos said one priority for the new agency is upgrading its data and technology capabilities. That will help tackle a broader issue: Quality day care and preschool programs are not equally distributed across the state, according to a report issued earlier this year by The Civic Federation, a taxpayer watchdog group.</p><p>“We have been working to build our data infrastructure so we can understand where children and families are receiving programs and where they're not so that we can make better informed decisions about where to put increased investments over time,” Ramos said.</p><p>During the next phase of the transition, the agency will work to move away from paper-and-pencil records. Small groups of parents, providers, educators and staff will test electronic systems before they are rolled out statewide. Ramos said the agency hopes to launch some of those upgrades within the next year.</p><p>The agency plans to hold regular transition meetings to collect feedback and track its progress. And it established a new family engagement team to help parents navigate the system.</p><p>“It is a new era for early childhood services in Illinois,” Ramos said.</p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wkiuudk-l-ti/" target="_blank" >Mariah Rush</a></h5><p>Screams, laughter and frequent groans could be heard on a recent visit to Parlay Lincoln Park.</p><p>The sports bar was packed with people, mostly millennials and younger, who were brought together by one thing: A particularly raunchy episode of "Love Island USA" — Peacock's dating reality TV series that airs six days a week.</p><p>The show has created such a buzz that many Chicago bars and restaurants have started hosting watch parties, themed nights and trivia — an effort to capitalize on a loyal and young fan base at a time when bars are struggling to draw in younger crowds during the week.</p><p>More than a dozen spots have advertised weekly watch parties for "Love Island USA." Some are selling tickets. </p><p>At Tacotlan in Hermosa, guests have been crowding into the back patio for watch parties twice a week. Owners of the BYOB restaurant say there are some requests to change the channel to World Cup games, but they're loyal to the "Love Island" fans.</p><p>"They’ve been watching, and they’ve been consistent. So the priority is going to be given to 'Love Island,'" owner Jessica Perjes said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wkiuudk-l-td/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>How do you keep cool amid a heat wave in Chicago?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Reply to this question via email</a> (please include your first and last name).
